question: Which genetic variants are associated with a trait or disease?

visscher2017.cite: Visscher et al. (2017). 10 Years of GWAS Discovery: Biology, Function, and Translation. American Journal of Human Genetics 101(1): 5–22.
visscher2017.checked: every quote read word for word in the PMC full text (PMC5501872), in Chrome, on 20 Nov 2026; places are its section headings, as the PMC page has no page numbers; in-text reference numbers are left out

steps.title: Gather people
steps.text: Collect DNA and the trait from many thousands of people: cases and controls, or a measured trait such as height.

quotes.text: The GWAS is an experimental design used to detect associations between genetic variants and traits in samples from populations.
quotes.where: section GWAS Rationale and Scientific Basis

steps.title: Test every variant
steps.text: Genotype each person at variants across the whole genome, often millions after imputation, then test each one for association with the trait, one test per variant.

after.where: sections Introduction and GWAS Rationale and Scientific Basis

steps.title: Strict threshold
steps.text: With millions of tests, chance alone gives thousands of p values below 0.05. Only p below 5 × 10⁻⁸ counts as genome-wide significant.

quotes.text: where “strong” is defined as statistically significant at the genome-wide p value threshold of 5 × 10−8

steps.title: Replicate
steps.text: Check the hits in independent samples. Well-powered GWAS hits have held up.

quotes.text: GWAS associations have proven highly replicable, both within and between populations, under the assumption of adequate sample sizes.

steps.title: Locus to biology
steps.text: A hit marks a region, not a gene or a mechanism. Finding which gene and how is further work.

quotes.text: an association between a genetic variant at a genomic locus and a trait is not directly informative with respect to the target gene or the mechanism whereby the variant is associated with phenotypic differences.
quotes.where: section GWAS Rationale and Scientific Basis

low-power.text: For example, for such rare variants with an effect size of 1 phenotypic standard deviation unit (about 7 cm for height or 5 BMI units), a sample size of more than one million is required
low-power.where: section GWAS Rationale and Scientific Basis

exercise.title: Why 5 × 10⁻⁸?
exercise.intro: Test many variants that have no effect at all, and count how many look significant at each threshold.
exercise.data_label: Example data, simulated for this exercise with a seeded random generator: every variant is null, so every hit is false. Real variants are correlated with their neighbours, so a real scan has fewer independent tests than variants.
